item.title: Solana plunges as geopolitical tensions overshadow Alpenglow upgrade amid macroeconomic concerns
item.description:
Solana came under renewed pressure as escalating Middle East tensions weighed on risk sentiment, with reports of US military preparations for potential strikes on Iran adding to concerns about another direct confrontation.

The combination of rising oil prices, growing economic concerns and a hawkish Federal Reserve creates a very challenging backdrop for the crypto market. If the conflict escalates further, SOL could remain vulnerable to a broader risk-off move.

Solana has also completed the Alpenglow upgrade which went live on mainnet on October 21, replacing TowerBFT and targeting transaction finality of around 150 milliseconds, down from approximately 12.8 seconds.

Looking ahead, tomorrow's US Flash PMIs could trigger further volatility given the lingering growth concerns. Weaker than expected data could intensify growth fears, weigh further on risk sentiment and trigger another selloff in SOL. Stronger data, on the other hand, might ease the concerns and lead to a short-term relief rally, although it wouldn’t change the bigger picture as it would just reinforce the need for further Fed tightening, thus limiting the recovery.

 

SOLANA TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see that Solanais back under pressure as renewed Middle East tensions weighed on risk sentiment. We have a key support zone around the 97.00 level. If the price gets there, we can expect the buyers to step in, with a defined risk below the support, to position for a rally into the 148.00 level. The sellers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking lower to increase the bearish bets into the major upward trendline next.

 

SOLANA TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 4 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 4 hour chart, we have a minor support zone around the 103.50 level. We can expect the dip-buyers to step in here, with a defined risk below the support, to keep targeting the resistance zone around the 113.00 level. The sellers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking lower to extend the drop into the 97.00 support.

 

SOLANA TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 1 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 1 hour chart, we have a minor downward trendline defining the current bearish momentum. The sellers will likely continue to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to keep pushing into the 97.00 support. The buyers, on the other hand, will look for a break higher to pile in for a rally into the 113.00 level next. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

UPCOMING CATALYSTS

item.title: EUR/CHF falls to three-month lows as French bond turmoil raises fresh euro risks
item.description:
It might not seem like it, but the euro is finding itself in a rather uncomfortable spot in trading today. While EUR/USD is holding up relatively better amid the broader market turmoil, EUR/CHF is perhaps telling us a more worrying story about the risks building in Europe.

The latest drop today sees the pair briefly touch its lowest level in three months, slipping to 0.9220 levels now as the Swiss franc draws renewed support from its traditional safe-haven appeal. But what is driving that?

Well, it's the thing we have been talking about every so often in the past two weeks, that being France's fiscal plight. And the worries are now growing rather quickly as French 10-year government bond yields have surged above 5%, hitting their highest levels since 2002.

Besides that, the France-Germany 10-year yield spread is now widening towards a staggering 170 bps - its highest since 2011. It wasn't just too long ago that we were talking the line in the sand at 150 bps. All of a sudden, we're now nearly 20 bps up from that. The latest surge is another sign that investors are demanding a much higher premium to hold French debt, amid growing fiscal and political uncertainty.

Looking at the EUR/CHF chart, we're already seeing some of those worries translate into price action. After all, France is Europe's second-largest economy and concerns there will have the potential to spill over into broader European assets and the euro.

The pair has already broken below its trendline support from the March to May lows, before surrendering the key 0.9300 level as the 100-day moving average (red line) also gave way. And the latest decline is now also challenging to break the 200-day moving average (blue line) around 0.9235.

A sustained break below that could invite a deeper push towards 0.9200 initially, before the June to July lows may offer a bit of support around 0.9180. Beyond that, the next notable downside level sits closer to 0.9100.

As for the Swiss franc side of the equation, let's not forget that the SNB had only recently toned down its language on foreign exchange intervention. The central bank hinted at less urgency to push back against franc strength. But with European risks now escalating and EUR/CHF threatening a more meaningful technical breakdown, I wonder if policymakers might soon have to reconsider that stance.

For now though, the EUR/CHF chart is certainly not giving the euro much reason for comfort as it arguably best captures the risks surrounding European bond markets.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: US futures tumble as AI rally faces fresh scrutiny despite solid Meta earnings
item.description:
US futures are taking quite a beating today as what looked to be a promising rebound in Wall Street yesterday is already threatening to unravel. S&P 500 futures are down 1% with Nasdaq futures down 1.7% as tech shares are bearing the brunt of the selling.

Tensions in the Middle East are once again pushing up oil prices, so that is arguably keeping investors on edge. But then, you have Treasury yields falling as 10-year yields are down to 5.08% today. Ordinarily, that should offer some relief to tech shares amid their lofty valuations. But not today, it seems.

In any case, I would argue that the bigger problem lies with earnings and whether the AI rally can continue to live up to the enormous expectations already priced in.

Now, Meta's earnings did at least offer some encouragement with revenue jumping 26% to $64.6 billion and its shares holding up relatively well. Shares are trading about 0.8% higher in after-hours trading but that optimism isn't translating into broader confidence across the tech sector.

Just look at Lam Research. The semiconductor equipment maker reported record quarterly revenue of around $8.2 billion, beating estimates, yet its shares have tumbled by over 8% in after-hours trading. Even a strong quarter wasn't enough as investors chose to focus on the weaker-than-expected forward earnings forecast instead.

Besides that, there's also Tesla getting into trouble after its own earnings release with shares down roughly 5% in after-hours trading. Meanwhile, smaller semiconductor firm NVE Corporation is seeing its shares sink by over 22% after reporting an 8% decline in quarterly revenue.

These are rather different earnings stories but collectively, they paint a picture of a market that is becoming much less forgiving. Much, much less.

And I think the bond market is also telling us something here. With Treasury yields falling even as oil prices rise, could investors be starting to worry more about US economic growth than inflation?

You might think that if yields are easing, it would help provide some comfort for stocks. However, that sort of relationship is not exactly straighforward. If yields are falling because investors are becoming nervous about the economic outlook, then the implications for corporate earnings and the stock market outlook are hardly encouraging as well.

For the AI trade, the latest market mood simply reinforces the narrative that investor expectations are becoming much harder to justify especially when the economy starts losing momentum. In particular, companies with heavy borrowing finance their AI ambitions are arguably the ones that will be hit the hardest.

Now, I wouldn't call this the end of the AI rally just yet. But when record earnings and falling Treasury yields can't provide much support to equities, it may be a case that Wall Street is finally starting to question whether the bar has been set too high. And waking up to that very reality could end up being extremely painful.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: European stock market open: Stocks tumble as French debt worries and bond yields weigh on sentiment
item.description:

  • Eurostoxx -1.5%
  • Germany DAX -1.0%
  • France CAC 40 -1.4%
  • UK FTSE 100 -0.5%
  • Spain IBEX -1.4%

It's an ugly one as the calmer mood from yesterday has totally been wiped out. While the selling is only returning today, the warning signs have been there all through the week - especially in the bond market.

French borrowing costs are once again surging, with 10-year yields pushing above the 5% level for the first time since 2002. Meanwhile, the France-Germany 10-year yield spread has pushed beyond 160 bps now, reaching levels last seen during the Eurozone debt crisis.

As such, that is hardly a comforting backdrop for European equities, especially when investors are already having to contend with elevated global bond yields and persistent geopolitical uncertainty.

And just a heads up to France's plight in that it might get worse, with Moody's set to review the country's sovereign credit rating tomorrow. The possibility of a downgrade is certainly something that is adding to market nerves today.

In any case, it's not just a French story that is weighing on the overall risk backdrop. Asian equities had it rough also earlier today and US futures are not faring any better. S&P 500 futures are down 1% with Nasdaq futures down 1.7% as AI worries continue to weigh on the overall mood. And that says quite a bit about how fragile the market confidence is, despite the better showing at the start of this month.

For now, the immediate concern is whether the latest selling will gather further momentum. And with bond yields staying elevated and little sign of a meaningful resolution to France's fiscal troubles, I wouldn't be counting on investors rushing back in to buy the dip just yet.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

Tomorrow’s US Flash PMIs could be an important catalyst. If the data surprises to the downside, growth concerns might increase and we could see a dovish repricing further out the curve. item.title: France business confidence improves in October but cracks remain beneath the surface
item.description:
• France October business confidence 97 vs 96 expected
  • Prior 96
  • France October industrial confidence 105
  • Prior 101
  • France October services confidence 99
  • Prior 98

The overall business climate picked up slightly in October but remains below the long-term average estimate of 100 for yet another month. For some context, the last time the business confidence index met the key level was all the way back in June 2024.

While there are improvements in confidence levels for both the manufacturing and services sectors, the report is not all sunshine and rainbows. Retail trade confidence fell by 3 points to 93 in October, marking the lowest estimate since June. Meanwhile, the employment index also fell significantly to 95 - its lowest since May. INSEE notes that the drop in the employment climate is due to the decrease in the balance related to expected workforce size in services (except temporary work).

Overall, the headline improvement is not exactly an optimistic signal that the French economy is back on the up. The details reveal that businesses are becoming less willing to hire, so that doesn't exactly inspire confidence in the outlook for household spending either - especially when retail sentiment is already looking rather fragile.

Then there's the broader fiscal backdrop to consider. French borrowing costs have been surging, with 10-year yields briefly climbing above 5% this week and the yield spread against Germany widening to levels not seen in roughly 15 years.

So while the headline improvement offers a tad bit of relief, I wouldn't get too carried away. France still has plenty of economic and fiscal problems to work through, and this latest survey does little to suggest that the worst is behind it.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Is EUR/USD giving traders a false sense of security as euro risks mount?
item.description:
If you look at EUR/USD this week, it may be easy to think that the euro is holding up and brushing aside the warning signals from the bond market. But in taking a step back, you might find that perhaps EUR/USD is not giving markets the full picture of the risks surrounding the euro at the moment.

The currency pair is holding up decently this week, trading around 1.1240 levels today after bouncing off support near 1.1200 on Monday. However, I wouldn't want to mistake that resilience for a sign that traders are becoming more comfortable with Europe's underlying problems.

I mean, the fact of the matter is that the bond market is telling us quite the opposite. The France-Germany 10-year yield spread has now widened to around 161 basis points, its highest since 2011.

As a reminder, this spread essentially tells us how much extra compensation that investors are demanding to lend money to France rather than Germany. And with France already struggling with fiscal uncertainty, political instability, and rising borrowing costs, that premium is becoming more and more difficult to ignore.

And yet, we're not seeing the same kind of urgency in EUR/USD this week. Puzzling, eh?

Looking at the daily chart, the pair is still in a tough spot in keeping below the key daily moving averages and managing just a light bounce after hitting a low of 1.1113 last week. But now, the recovery attempt is seeing the pair test resistance around 1.1250-60 with the 23.6 Fib retracement level at 1.1254 in focus. But still, there's little reason to suggest that the broader technical picture has improved significantly unless buyers can break through that and look to test 1.1340-50 levels next.

Having said that, it is not to say that sellers are firmly in control to pressure the pair lower in chasing a further downside break below 1.1200 currently. So, what gives?

Well, perhaps the more telling chart right now is EUR/CHF.

The pair has already broken below its trendline support from the March to May lows, alongside the 100-day moving average (red line) near 0.9300 earlier this month. And now, sellers are putting pressure on the 200-day moving average (blue line) around 0.9235. A sustained break below that could open the door towards 0.9200 initially, before putting the 0.9000 level back into focus.

Considering that the franc tends to benefit when investors become more defensive about European risks, EUR/CHF might actually be the best indication of how traders are pricing in euro risks at the moment. And from the chart, they are saying that the euro might be on the verge of a steeper decline if things continue.

Circling back to EUR/USD, the fact that dollar sentiment is also another big part of the equation is perhaps why the pair hasn't been the best gauge of euro risks this week. The dollar has struggled in the past few sessions as Treasury yields are sticking with the sharp pullback from last week. 10-year yields are still at 5.09% today, nearly unchanged from the start of the week itself.

So if you're looking for signs that traders are growing more uncomfortable with Europe's fiscal outlook, I would argue that EUR/CHF and the French-German yield spread deserve far more attention than EUR/USD alone right now.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Chart of the day: Gold price falls below $4,100 as sellers threaten another breakdown
item.description:
Uh oh. Gold is starting to find itself in a bit of a pickle again in trading this week, with price now falling below $4,100 today as sellers look to try and tighten their grip on the precious metal.

The setup for gold over the past few weeks has been defined by the range around $4,100 to $4,200 for the most part. And yesterday, we started to see price action invite a test of the downside range. Today, that very floor is now being threatened and buyers are surely starting to sweat now when you look at how things are playing out.

As things stand, the broader fundamental backdrop remains challenging for gold. While Treasury yields are not returning to multi-decade highs yet, they are still at elevated levels which are keeping a non-yielding asset like gold in a tough position. Then, you have the renewed surge in oil prices only adding to inflation worries and keeping expectations for further Fed tightening alive. That is not quite the combination that will do gold any good.

But even putting all of that aside, the technical picture itself is rather worrying.

Since the drop in late September, any recovery attempts in gold this month have been repeatedly capped around $4,200. The 100-day moving average (red line) also adds another layer in limiting any meaningful recovery, although we haven't even seen buyers gather enough conviction to test that in recent weeks.

So, that leaves us with the more immediate concern now and that is the downside floor around the $4,100-17 region. We are seeing another test below $4,100 today and will it be a case of third time being the charm for sellers in breaking through?

A firm daily close well below $4,100 would leave the door open for a further decline towards the psychological $4,000 mark. And below that, the July low around $3,960 would be the next key downside target.

As for buyers, reclaiming $4,200 remains the most important step towards easing the immediate selling pressure. But with both key daily moving averages still sitting well above current prices, the broader technical outlook continues to favour sellers.

As such, I'd be more concerned about support giving way than betting on another rebound - at least for the time being.

Where could XAUUSD go from here? Watch this week's Exness Trade of the Week for the key market factors and possible scenarios.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: US-Iran tensions refuse to fade as fresh Strait of Hormuz attacks keep oil markets on edge
item.description:
While we haven't seen things escalate further recently, it is best to be reminded that US-Iran tensions are still very much simmering beneath the surface. And the IRGC is offering a reminder of that as they claim that four vessels were hit and caught fire in the northern Gulf, while three other vessels were reportedly struck by mines west of the Strait of Hormuz overnight.

Besides that, Tehran is also warning that its response could extend to US bases across the region if Washington continues to encourage vessels to cross the Strait of Hormuz.

The major concern here remains the fact that shipping through one of the world's most important energy routes remains vulnerable to further disruption. And even if oil supplies continue to flow, the threat alone is enough to keep shipping costs elevated and place a geopolitical premium into oil prices. So, that is hardly the kind of environment which will allow for oil markets to settle down comfortably.

With that in mind, the situation also leaves broader market sentiment walking on eggshells.

Sure, investors have not paid all too much attention to US-Iran developments as of late amid a lack of meaningful progress or escalation. However, the continued tensions and just the risk of things blowing up further could quickly bring oil prices, inflation worries, and risk aversion back into focus. Just the very fact that the threat continues to hang over the shoulders of broader markets is enough to make things difficult for investors in the bigger picture.

So until there are clearer signs of de-escalation, I wouldn't be too quick to dismiss the geopolitical risks lurking in the background. And we might very well have to wait until the US midterm elections are over and done with before we find out what Trump wants to do next in the conflict here.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: The Floor 8 Moves From Launch Into Its Next Phase of Growth
item.description:
The Floor 8 is entering a new phase of development, building on its launch with an ambition to make trading programs more accessible to eligible traders worldwide.

This next chapter brings together two priorities: accelerating the brand’s growth and strengthening the operational foundations that support the trader experience.

At the center of that strategy is the firm’s 50/50 Evaluation, a model designed to reduce the upfront financial commitment required to begin an evaluation.

A More Accessible Starting Point

The 50/50 Evaluation divides the program fee into two payments. Traders pay half upfront, with the remaining half payable only after successfully completing the evaluation and choosing to activate their funded account.

For traders who do not pass, the second payment is never due.

The approach reflects a straightforward philosophy: giving traders an opportunity to demonstrate their ability before committing the full evaluation fee.

By changing when the fee is paid, The Floor 8 aims to create a more accessible starting point for traders seeking a clearly defined path into its simulated funded programs.

Flexibility Within a Clear Framework

The payment structure is supported by evaluation conditions designed to give traders flexibility in how they approach their objectives.

The 50/50 Evaluation features no daily drawdown rule, no floating-loss rule and no minimum trading days during evaluation. Traders may pass in a single trade if they reach the profit target and meet all applicable requirements.

For eligible traders who prefer to skip the evaluation stage, The Floor 8 also offers an Instant Funded program, providing another entry option into its simulated trading environment.

 

 

Building the Operation Behind the Brand

As The Floor 8 moves beyond launch, its focus extends to the infrastructure and people supporting its programs.

Trading technology, customer support, risk oversight and back-office coordination form the foundation of that work. The objective is to deliver a consistent experience across registration, account access, trading and ongoing support.

The firm’s growth ambitions are tied to developing those capabilities, incorporating trader feedback and refining the experience as its international reach expands.

The Vision of a Modern Trading Floor

Summary:

  • Oil edged slightly higher and gold fell, as reports pointed to US and Israeli preparations for renewed strikes on Iran
  • The US dollar weakened against the euro, Swiss franc, sterling, yen and Canadian dollar, while the Australian and New Zealand dollars dipped
  • New Zealand Q3 CPI slowed to 3.7%, below the 3.8% forecast, but markets still price a near-certain RBNZ hike next week
  • The Bank of Korea held its benchmark rate at 3.00%, as expected, after back-to-back hikes in July and August
  • Regional equities mostly fell: the Hang Seng dropped about 2.5%, the Nikkei 225 and Shanghai Composite lost around 1%, and the Kospi fell more than the Nikkei
  • Meta beat revenue and earnings forecasts and its shares rose, while Tesla climbed to three-month highs on strong margins and free cash flow

Main article:

Asian markets delivered a mixed session on Thursday, with regional equities mostly lower, the US dollar softer against most major currencies and oil edging higher as reports pointed to renewed US and Israeli military planning against Iran. News flow was relatively light, with much of the session’s coverage focused on outlooks and analyst views.

Geopolitics remained the main backdrop for commodities. The New York Times reported that the US and Israeli militaries have drawn up plans for a short but intensive round of strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections. It noted, however, that President Donald Trump has repeatedly called off planned attacks this year. NBC News separately reported that the US is reducing troop numbers at Middle East bases and cutting diplomatic staff in the region, after the State Department ordered non-emergency personnel to leave Saudi Arabia. Oil prices tracked slightly higher, while gold fell.

In currency markets, the US dollar mostly weakened, losing ground against the euro, Swiss franc, British pound, Japanese yen and Canadian dollar. The Australian and New Zealand dollars bucked the trend and dipped.

The New Zealand dollar slipped after third-quarter inflation came in slightly below expectations. Annual CPI slowed to 3.7% from 4.1%, under both the 3.8% consensus and the Reserve Bank of New Zealand’s 3.9% projection, while quarterly prices rose 0.7%. Inflation remains above the RBNZ’s 1% to 3% target, and markets continue to price a near-certain rate hike at next week’s policy review, with economists expecting inflation to pick up again in the fourth quarter as fuel prices rise.

The Bank of Korea held its benchmark rate at 3.00%, as all analysts surveyed by Reuters had expected, pausing after quarter-point hikes in July and August. Economists see a further increase to 3.25% in November as likely, given strong chip-driven exports and above-target inflation.

Regional equities were broadly weaker. Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell around 1%, while South Korea’s Kospi posted steeper losses. In China, the Shanghai Composite dropped about 1%, extending a 10 week fall, and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng underperformed with a fall of around 2.5%.

On the corporate front, Meta Platforms reported third-quarter revenue and earnings per share ahead of forecasts, and its shares rose, although operating income was weighed by a $9.9 billion legal charge. The company also announced plans for an effective 2-for-1 stock split through a new class of non-voting shares. Tesla shares climbed to three-month highs after the company beat expectations on gross margin and free cash flow, and set a target of producing about 5 million vehicles a year by 2030.

item.title: Kinder Morgan commits to $4.2B Texas gas pipeline to fuel hyperscale data center power
item.description:
The deal shows hyperscalers are now willing to underwrite long-term fuel infrastructure, not just compute, to secure power. That reinforces natural gas as the main bridge fuel for the AI build-out. For the gas market, Permian Link adds about 2.8 billion cubic feet a day of takeaway capacity from the Permian Basin. That should help ease pipeline constraints that have periodically pushed local Waha gas prices deeply negative, while lifting structural demand for US gas over the decade. Midstream operators with Permian and Southeast exposure are likely to benefit from a growing pipeline of data centre and utility contracts. Long-dated take-or-pay commitments make their earnings more predictable. The 2030 start dates highlight a timing gap, however: data centres coming online before then will still compete for existing grid and gas capacity, which keeps near-term pressure on power prices in key hubs.

---

Contrast with Australia yesterday:

  • NEXTDC shares plunge 44% as power delays expose AI data centre bottleneck

---

The AI boom is now laying steel in the ground: a hyperscaler has locked in 20 years of gas supply through a new Texas pipeline, a sign that data centres are building their own power supply chains.

Summary:

  • Kinder Morgan formally committed to Permian Link, a $4.2 billion joint venture pipeline, with its share at about $1.6 billion
  • The roughly 434-mile line will carry about 2.8 bcf/d of gas from the Permian Basin to the Midcontinent, serving power demand in the Texas Panhandle, from 2030
  • The anchor customer is power providers serving an unnamed A-rated hyperscale data centre operator, under a 20-year take-or-pay contract
  • Kinder Morgan also approved the Southeast Connector, with its share at about $3.1 billion, adding up to 2.6 bcf/d for utilities from 2030 to 2032
  • Q3 adjusted EPS of 35 cents beat the 32-cent estimate, and the project backlog rose to $14.4 billion from $9.6 billion
  • Executives said other customers have shown interest beyond the anchor hyperscaler, and Southeast large-load interconnection requests exceed 200 GW

Kinder Morgan has formally committed to building a $4.2 billion natural gas pipeline across West Texas and the Panhandle to help power a hyperscale data centre complex, as surging electricity demand from artificial intelligence drives a new wave of US energy infrastructure.

The Permian Link project, a joint venture on Kinder Morgan’s Natural Gas Pipeline Company of America system, will carry about 2.8 billion cubic feet of gas a day along roughly 434 miles of new pipe, from the Permian Basin near Pecos County to NGPL’s Midcontinent system. Kinder Morgan’s share of the cost is about $1.6 billion, and the line is expected to enter service in 2030. The gas will move north to serve power demand in the Texas Panhandle, and the project links to storage to improve reliability.

The anchor customer is power providers serving an unnamed A-rated hyperscale data centre operator, under a 20-year take-or-pay contract. Under that type of agreement, the customer pays for reserved capacity whether or not it uses it. Executives said other customers have also shown interest.

The project was announced alongside the Southeast Connector, on Kinder Morgan’s Southern Natural Gas system, where its share is about $3.1 billion. That line will add up to 2.6 bcf/d of capacity for investment-grade utilities, entering service in phases from 2030 to 2032, and could be expanded if more customers sign. Management cited more than 200 GW of large-load interconnection requests in the Southeast. Together, Kinder Morgan’s share of the two projects is about $4.7 billion, a commitment it linked to rising demand from power plants, data centres and LNG exporters.

The broader implications for data centres are significant. Securing reliable power has become one of the biggest constraints on the AI build-out, and a hyperscaler signing a 20-year fuel contract suggests operators are increasingly willing to lock in their own long-term energy supply rather than rely solely on the grid. Long-term gas supply also supports on-site and dedicated gas-fired generation, which can be built faster than many grid upgrades. That could help unlock new data centre sites in regions such as the Texas Panhandle, where land and gas are abundant.

The announcements came with third-quarter results that beat expectations. Adjusted earnings per share rose 21% to 35 cents, ahead of the 32-cent consensus, and the project backlog climbed to $14.4 billion from $9.6 billion, with natural gas projects at a record $13.2 billion. Kinder Morgan said full-year results are on track to exceed its budget.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Most analysts now expect the next BOJ rate hike in December, none see October move: Bloomberg
item.description:
With an October 30 move ruled out by every economist surveyed, the yen’s direction is likely to hinge on the tone of the BOJ’s statement and outlook report. A declaration that underlying inflation has reached 2% would mark a historic shift and strengthen expectations of a December hike. That could support the yen and push Japanese government bond yields higher. Board voting is another swing factor: further dissent from Takaichi-appointed members would likely weigh on the yen, while a call for a hike by a hawkish member would have the opposite effect. Oil prices remain a key influence on Japan’s inflation outlook as a major energy importer. Any escalation in the Middle East that lifts crude would add to the case for steady quarterly hikes, while also pressuring Japan’s trade balance and the yen.

---

Earlier:

  • BOJ seen lifting rates to 1.50% in December as 69% of economists expect a Q4 hike

---

BOJ watchers have moved firmly toward a December hike, and the bigger question this month is whether Japan’s central bank finally declares victory on 2% inflation after 13 years of trying.

Summary:

  • 83% of economists surveyed by Bloomberg expect the Bank of Japan’s next rate hike in December, up from 35% a month ago, when January was the most popular pick
  • None expect a move at the October 30 meeting; the policy rate stands at 1.25%
  • 67% now expect the BOJ to hike every three months, up from 46%, and the median terminal rate forecast is unchanged at 1.75%
  • The key focus in October is whether the BOJ judges that underlying inflation has reached its 2% target, which it has not declared since setting the goal in 2013
  • About two-thirds of economists think Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s government has softened its stance on rate hikes, after the US urged Japan to drop reflationary policies
  • September’s hike drew two dissents from Takaichi-appointed board members, keeping voting patterns in focus

More than 80% of Bank of Japan watchers now expect the central bank’s next interest rate increase to come in December, according to a Bloomberg survey, with none forecasting a move when its next meeting concludes on October 30.

Some 83% of economists expect the BOJ to raise borrowing costs from 1.25% at its meeting ending December 18, up sharply from 35% in last month’s survey, when January was the most popular pick. Two-thirds of respondents also expect the BOJ to hike every three months, up from 46%. That suggests economists see it maintaining its current pace after September’s increase, its second in three months and the fastest tightening since 1990. The median forecast for the peak rate in this cycle held at 1.75%.

Many economists said the main focus of this month’s meeting will be whether the BOJ concludes that underlying inflation has reached its 2% target, something it has not declared since adopting the goal in 2013. Economists at Morgan Stanley MUFG Securities expect the bank to signal that underlying inflation is around 2%, and to deliver a hawkish hold. Economists expect the quarterly outlook report released alongside the decision to leave inflation projections broadly unchanged, apart from a slight upgrade for next fiscal year.

September’s hike took the policy rate into the BOJ’s estimated neutral range of 1.1% to 2.5% for the first time, increasing market interest in how high rates will ultimately go.

Politics remains a factor. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is known as a supporter of monetary easing. However, after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urged Japan to drop reflationary policies, Takaichi and her ministers said they are not pursuing reflation. About two-thirds of economists in the survey now think the government has softened its stance on BOJ hikes. Strategists at Mitsubishi UFJ Morgan Stanley Securities said the prime minister’s office probably does not welcome further increases, but is likely to tacitly accept them for now, largely because of relations with the US.

Board votes are also under scrutiny. September’s increase drew dissents from Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato, both Takaichi appointees, which helped weaken the yen. Some economists see a chance that hawkish board member Hajime Takata will push for a back-to-back hike at this month’s meeting.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Musk races to seal $3.7 trillion SpaceX-Tesla merger before Trump exits, Bloomberg says
item.description:
A target window for an announcement by mid-2027 gives the merger speculation a timeline. That is likely to keep Tesla shares sensitive to any headlines from the special committees, and SpaceX shares sensitive to swings in AI sentiment, since its stock would be the deal currency. A sustained selloff in chip and AI stocks is the key market risk to the deal: it would weaken SpaceX’s valuation leverage and the investor enthusiasm needed for a transaction of this size. The midterm elections on November 3 add a political variable, as a Democratic win in either chamber could bring closer scrutiny of Musk’s businesses. For broader markets, a combination on this scale would intensify focus on AI-related capital spending and cash burn, at a time when investors are already questioning when that investment will pay off.

---

Earlier:

  • JPMorgan doubles SpaceX target to $500 on AI growth, maps out possible Tesla merger

---

Musk has said he wants SpaceX and Tesla together, and now the race is on to get the biggest deal in corporate history done while the White House is friendly and investors are still believers.

Summary:

  • There is a push to announce a SpaceX-Tesla merger by the first half of 2027 so it can close during the Trump administration, Bloomberg (gated) reported, citing people familiar with the matter
  • A combination would bring together companies worth around $3.7 trillion, the largest corporate transaction ever attempted
  • Musk called the deal a good idea but said he would recuse himself, leaving special committees to work through terms, which have not been settled
  • Musk controls more than 80% of SpaceX’s voting power but owns about 20% of Tesla, making Tesla shareholder approval the tougher hurdle
  • Risks to the timeline include the midterm elections and a possible sustained selloff in chip and AI stocks
  • JPMorgan flagged tension between SpaceX’s national security contracts and Tesla’s large China manufacturing footprint for regulatory and shareholder approval

Elon Musk’s backers are racing to secure a merger of SpaceX and Tesla while political and market conditions remain favourable, with a push to announce a deal by the first half of 2027 so it can close during President Donald Trump’s administration, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

The combination would bring together companies with a combined market value of around $3.7 trillion, making it the largest corporate transaction ever attempted. Musk gave his strongest public endorsement yet on SpaceX’s earnings call this week, describing a combination as a good idea. He said he would recuse himself and leave special committees at both companies to work through the details, cautioned that winning over Tesla shareholders could be difficult, and said no terms had been agreed. SpaceX and Tesla did not respond to Bloomberg’s requests for comment on the timing.

According to the report, timing will depend on when Tesla’s board is comfortable with the details. Shareholder approval is less of an obstacle at SpaceX, where Musk controls more than 80% of the voting power. At Tesla, where he owns about 20% of the stock, it will be harder. However, the board and shareholders approved a trillion-dollar pay package for him less than a year ago.

Two risks are shaping the timeline. The US midterm elections are less than two weeks away, and Democratic control of either chamber of Congress could open Musk and his companies to investigations while weakening a president nearing lame-duck status. A sustained selloff in chipmaker and AI stocks could also erode the investor support needed for the deal. SpaceX shares have recovered strongly after falling below their $135 IPO price following the June listing, rising 47% since August 5. Analysts say that makes SpaceX’s stock an attractive currency for a deal, though a fall in its price could complicate terms.

The companies already have business ties, most notably their joint Terafab semiconductor plant in Texas, and have been laying groundwork for closer cooperation, with AI as a common thread. Both are expected to burn billions of dollars a quarter for the foreseeable future, a sharp shift for Tesla, whose car business has generated steady cash in recent years.

JPMorgan said in a research note that the national security sensitivities around SpaceX’s US defence contracts, and Tesla’s large China manufacturing base, are key dynamics at odds with each other in winning regulatory and shareholder approval. In a separate note this week, the bank suggested any deal would likely be an all-stock transaction led by SpaceX.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bank of Korea holds rate at 3% after back-to-back hikes, keeps door open to November move
item.description:
With the hold fully priced, attention shifts to Governor Shin’s news conference at 02:10 GMT for guidance on whether November remains live. A clear signal that the pause is temporary would likely support the won and push short-dated Korean government bond yields higher. A softer emphasis on monitoring the impact of past hikes could weigh on the currency. The board’s caution over recent stock market volatility suggests policymakers are wary of adding pressure to equities, which may offer some relief for the KOSPI. Chipmakers remain at the centre of the growth story given record AI-driven exports. Energy prices are a key upside risk to inflation for Korea as a major oil importer. That leaves the outlook sensitive to any escalation in the Middle East that lifts crude.

---

Earlier (preview):

  • Bank of Korea expected to hold rates today after two hikes, tightening cycle seen intact

---The Bank of Korea has stopped to catch its breath rather than end its tightening, with record chip exports and sticky inflation keeping a November hike firmly in view.

Summary:

  • The Bank of Korea held its seven-day repo rate at 3.00%, as forecast by all 34 analysts in a Reuters poll
  • The decision follows quarter-point hikes in July and August, the central bank’s first consecutive increases in more than three years
  • Governor Shin Hyun Song has said policy will remain restrictive until inflation returns to target
  • Headline inflation slowed to 2.9% in September from 3.1% in August, still above the 2% target
  • Exports for January to September topped $800 billion for the first time, driven by global AI spending
  • The median forecast in the Reuters survey sees a hike to 3.25% in November, in line with the central bank’s dot plot

The Bank of Korea left its benchmark interest rate unchanged on Thursday, pausing after back-to-back quarter-point hikes, though strong chip-driven growth and above-target inflation keep further tightening on the table.

The seven-member monetary policy board voted to hold the seven-day repurchase rate at 3.00%, Reuters reported, a decision forecast by all 34 analysts in its survey. The central bank raised rates in July and August, its first consecutive increases in more than three years. Governor Shin Hyun Song said afterward that a gradual pace of tightening was preferred.

Shin reiterated at an International Monetary Fund event on October 13 that policy will stay restrictive until inflation converges with the central bank’s target. Analysts said ahead of the meeting that a pause would slow the pace of tightening and soften its hawkish intensity. They noted the central bank had committed to monitoring the effects of its back-to-back hikes, and that recent market volatility, particularly in equities, made a hawkish decision less likely.

Headline consumer inflation slowed to 2.9% in September from 3.1% in August but remains above the Bank of Korea’s 2% target. Growth is being driven by exports, which are benefiting from global spending on artificial intelligence. Shipments for January to September exceeded $800 billion for the first time on record, underscoring the strength of South Korea’s semiconductor sector.

With growth expected to stay firm and inflation above target, the median forecast in the Reuters survey points to a hike to 3.25% at the Bank of Korea’s November meeting. That would be in line with the central bank’s own dot plot projection, which sets out policymakers’ expected path for rates.

The decision means the pause is likely to be read as a change in pace rather than direction. Markets will look to Shin’s news conference, due at 02:10 GMT, for signals on whether policymakers see a November hike as the most likely next step, and how they weigh firm growth and inflation against recent financial market volatility. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Iran’s floating oil reserves in Asia run dry under US naval blockade, WSJ reports
item.description:
For the oil market, the loss of Iranian barrels is being offset by non-Iranian Gulf supply, which is flowing through the Strait of Hormuz above prewar levels under US protection. That helps explain why the depletion is not by itself a fresh supply shock. The more immediate effect is a reshuffling of trade flows: Chinese refiners, particularly independents that relied on discounted Iranian crude, are buying more from Brazil and West Africa, which could tighten Atlantic Basin grades and lift their premiums. The bigger risk is escalation. With its main revenue source shut off, Tehran has fewer economic options and more incentive to use energy disruption as leverage, which keeps a geopolitical risk premium in crude. Any move to strike Gulf energy infrastructure or shipping would hit physical supply directly, rather than just sentiment.

---

Earlier:

  • US and Israel plan specific renewed Iran strikes after US midterms, New York Times reports

---

Iran’s floating oil piggy bank off Southeast Asia is empty, leaving Tehran’s war economy with its biggest cash source cut off and few good options left.

Summary:

  • Iran’s offshore crude reserves held in Asian waters were fully depleted by mid-October under the US naval blockade, according to ship-tracking analysts cited by the Wall Street Journal
  • US Central Command says the blockade has denied Iran at least $25 billion in oil revenue, limiting its ability to replace weapons and factories
  • Oil sales account for about 30% to 40% of Iranian government revenue and are its largest source of foreign exchange
  • The floating reserves, which peaked at nearly 90 million barrels, fell below 1 million barrels by October 5
  • Chinese refiners are increasingly turning to alternative suppliers, including Brazil and West Africa
  • Non-Iranian oil exports from the Gulf have recently exceeded prewar levels under US protection through the Strait of Hormuz

Iran’s stockpile of crude oil held on tankers in Asian waters has run dry under the US naval blockade, cutting off a key source of cash for Tehran during the war, the Wall Street Journal (gated) reported.

Ship-tracking analysts said the floating reserves, mostly held off the coasts of Malaysia and Singapore, were fully depleted by mid-October, because the blockade stopped Iran from replenishing the crude it normally sells to Chinese refineries. US Central Command said the blockade has denied Iran at least $25 billion in oil revenue, which it said would constrain Tehran’s ability to replace destroyed weapons and factories.

The floating storage was part of a long-running system Iran used to get oil to China despite US sanctions. Iranian-linked tankers carried crude to waters off Malaysia and Singapore and transferred it to other vessels bound for Chinese refineries, making the flows harder to track.

When the war began in February, Iran had around 135 million barrels stored overseas, likely worth $10 billion or more after oil prices surged. After the US first imposed a blockade in April, Iran kept selling from that reserve. When the blockade was lifted in mid-June as part of peace talks, Tehran rushed out more oil, rebuilding stocks to a peak of nearly 90 million barrels before the blockade was reimposed in mid-July. By October 5, reserves had fallen below 1 million barrels, and they have since been exhausted, according to analysts. Other trackers reported similarly sharp declines, with one estimating about 6 million barrels off Singapore as of October 9.

Oil sales account for roughly 30% to 40% of Iranian government revenue and are the country’s largest source of foreign exchange. Iran’s currency has lost about a third of its value against the dollar since early July, fuelling rapid inflation. Because Chinese payments can take around two months to arrive, Tehran may still receive some funds from past sales in the coming weeks. Analysts say overland routes such as trucking cannot replace seaborne exports.

Chinese refiners are increasingly turning to alternative suppliers, including Brazil and West Africa. Meanwhile, oil from elsewhere in the Middle East has recently exceeded prewar levels, as US protection helps secure non-Iranian shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran’s central bank governor, Abdolnaser Hemmati, said last week that the economy had shown resilience and rejected claims that it is collapsing. Analysts note Iran has so far defied predictions that the blockade would force it to make nuclear concessions. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitmine’s 5% hard cap leaves Ether’s biggest corporate buyer weeks from the exit
item.description:
The end of Bitmine’s buying removes a steady, price-insensitive source of ETH demand, but the bid has already faded to roughly a tenth of its May pace, so much of the adjustment is likely priced in. The bigger swing factor for ETH is whether spot ETF flows and broader risk appetite fill the gap left by treasury companies. A shift to selling staking rewards would add a small but persistent supply overhang. Bitmine shares now trade more on staking income and buybacks than on accumulation.

---

Earlier:

  • Bitcoin shows some buying life as risk-on flows return and push the digital currency higher
  • Bitcoin rallies on US-Iran deal hopes amid increasingly positive reports. What's next?

---

Ether’s most reliable corporate buyer is about to stop, but the market has been weaning itself off Bitmine’s bid since May, so the real test is who steps in next.

Summary:

  • Tom Lee said at Token2049 that Bitmine will not hold more than 5% of Ether’s supply, turning a target into a hard cap
  • Bitmine held about 6.03 million ETH as of 11 October, or 4.9% of a total supply of around 122.1 million
  • That leaves the company roughly 76,000 ETH short, with recent buying pointing to the cap being reached around mid-to-late November
  • Weekly purchases have fallen from more than 111,000 ETH in May to around 12,500
  • About 5.07 million ETH is staked, and staking rewards could push holdings above 5% without new purchases
  • Lee argues the cap ends the need to raise capital and should help Bitmine shares outperform ETH in a rally

Bitmine Immersion Technologies, the largest corporate holder of Ether, is within weeks of ending a buying programme that has added ETH to its treasury every week since June 2025, after chairman Tom Lee turned the company’s long-standing 5% supply target into a firm ceiling. Speaking at the Token2049 conference in Singapore on 7 October, Lee said Bitmine would not accumulate beyond 5% of Ether’s supply, Cointelegraph reported. That marks a shift from earlier comments in which he left the door open to holding more if Ethereum adoption kept growing.

The company’s latest weekly update showed about 6.03 million ETH as of 11 October, or 4.9% of a total supply of roughly 122.1 million. That leaves it around 76,000 ETH short of the cap. At the pace of recent weeks, roughly 12,500 to 15,000 ETH a week, the target would be reached around mid-to-late November, though Bitmine holds more than $600 million in cash and marketable securities and could close the gap faster if it chose to.

For more than a year, Bitmine has been one of the most consistent sources of demand for ETH, buying through a market in which the token fell about 10% over the first nine months of 2026. The bid has already shrunk sharply, however. Weekly purchases topped 111,000 ETH in May, against roughly 12,500 in the week to 11 October. Much of the effect of Bitmine stepping back may therefore already be in the price, making the end of buying more a formal full stop than a sudden loss of demand.

Lee presents the cap as good news for shareholders, arguing that the company no longer needs to raise capital to buy ETH and that its shares should outperform the token in a rally. That is the company’s view rather than an established outcome, and the position was carrying an unrealised loss of around $4.5 billion near the time of the speech.

Staking adds a complication. About 5.07 million of Bitmine’s ETH is staked, meaning it is locked up to help secure the Ethereum network in return for rewards paid in new ETH. Those rewards can push holdings above 5% without any purchases. Lee has said the company could sell staking income to stay under the cap, but has also said he sees little reason to sell ETH, with staking income covering dividends on its preferred shares.

What to watch next: the weekly holdings updates, for the week Bitmine reports reaching 5% and stopping; whether it begins selling staking rewards, which would turn a steady buyer into a small, regular seller; and spot Ether ETF flows, to see whether other demand fills the gap. A marked slide in ETH once buying ends would suggest the treasury bid mattered more than its recent size implied, while a steady price would confirm the market had already moved on. Lee has revised his stance on the cap once already, so a strong rally could test it again. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Ray Dalio warns US bond bear market has a long way to go as debt supply swamps demand
item.description:
Dalio’s analysis points to sustained upward pressure on long-dated Treasury yields, as heavy issuance meets weakening demand from foreign buyers and a Fed buying mainly bills. That supports a steeper yield curve and keeps term premium in focus. His warning on Japanese repatriation is significant for currency markets: an unwind of currency-hedged Treasury holdings could support the yen and Japanese government bonds while adding to selling pressure on US debt. For credit, his focus on accelerating hyperscaler issuance and declining free cash flow suggests AI-linked corporate bonds may need to offer wider spreads to clear the market. Equities are the lagging risk in his framework: he sees stocks as vulnerable once higher yields start to bite, with a surge in AI-related equity supply adding to the strain. Reduced demand for US debt from Middle Eastern oil exporters ties the outlook partly to energy markets, as oil revenues shape their capacity to recycle surpluses into Treasuries.

-

Ray Dalio’s message is that the bond sell-off is not a passing storm but the middle of a cycle he mapped out last year, and the bill for stocks has not yet arrived.

Summary:

  • Ray Dalio says the US is in the mid-cycle stage where rates have risen sharply but have not yet hit stocks, credit spreads or the economy, and the bond bear market probably has much further to run
  • There is about $32 trillion of marketable Treasury debt, up 8% in a year, with about $2.1 trillion of net new issuance expected in 2026; bills now make up about half of issuance, against a historical target of about 20%
  • Foreign investors hold about $9.3 trillion of Treasuries, and Dalio sees Japan and China as having incentives to reduce holdings
  • Total government debt service, including principal rollovers, is around 200% of federal revenue, and interest costs are about 21% of revenue
  • Total US net fixed-income financing needs are seen at around $4.4 trillion in 2027, with corporate borrowing driven heavily by AI capex
  • Equity issuance surged to a $1.8 trillion annualised pace in the first half, led by the AI build-out, adding to the supply of financial assets

The US bond bear market probably has a long way to go, according to Bridgewater Associates founder Ray Dalio, who warns that the supply of debt and equity coming to market is far larger than investors can absorb without higher yields and lower prices.

In a new article, Dalio said developments since he published his book on how countries go broke in June 2025 have tracked his template closely. He argues the US is now in the middle of the cycle, where interest rates have risen sharply and central banks are tightening, but before those moves have hit stocks, credit spreads and economic activity. Historically, he said, rates keep rising at this stage until weakness in rate-sensitive markets and sectors starts to restore balance.

On supply, Dalio noted there is about $32 trillion of marketable Treasury debt outstanding, up 8% in a year, with about $2.1 trillion of net new issuance expected in 2026. Treasury has shifted heavily toward short-term bills, which now account for about half of issuance compared with a historical target of around 20%. He said this eases pressure on long-dated yields but raises rollover risk and makes interest costs more volatile.

On demand, Dalio said foreigners own about 32% of Treasuries and the Fed about 14%, and support is shifting toward domestic buyers. He highlighted China and Japan as the key holders to watch. Concerns over US debt, diversification into gold and fear of sanctions are reducing Chinese appetite, while Japan has incentives to repatriate capital to support the yen and its bond market. That could unwind currency-hedged carry trades in a disruptive way. Middle Eastern oil exporters are also buying less US debt, he said.

Debt service is the second pressure point. Dalio said the average rate on existing debt is about 3.5%, against market rates of 4% to 5.5%, so interest costs will keep climbing as debt rolls over even if rates stay put. A one percentage point rise would eventually add about $310 billion a year in interest. Total debt service, including principal rollovers, is around 200% of government revenue.

Dalio stressed that Treasury is competing with a surge in corporate borrowing driven by AI investment. He expects total US net fixed-income financing needs of around $4.4 trillion in 2027. He described hyperscaler bond issuance, which reached about $220 billion in the first half of 2026 against about $108 billion for all of 2025, as the canary in the coal mine. Rising capex is already eroding free cash flow and pushing up credit spreads.

Equity supply is surging too. Issuance hit a $1.8 trillion annualised pace in the first half, Dalio said, driven by AI-related IPOs, secondary offerings and private fundraising. Globally, OECD governments are expected to borrow about $18 trillion gross in 2026. Dalio concluded that the supply of financial assets appears much larger than demand can absorb, though he noted his views are not investment advice. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6756 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US and Israel plan specific renewed Iran strikes after US midterms, New York Times reports
item.description:
Oil is the market most exposed to this report. The planning points to a window for renewed strikes from early November, once US forces are fully in place, and that timing is likely to keep a geopolitical risk premium embedded in crude. Iran’s threat to target Saudi refineries, including Aramco facilities, specifically to drive up energy prices is a direct risk to physical supply, not just sentiment. Indications that US targeting may avoid oil infrastructure to limit pump price rises offer only partial reassurance, given that Iran would choose its own retaliation targets. Threats against data centres and undersea internet cables add a new technology dimension to the risk. Trump’s record of cancelling strikes at the last minute means markets may continue to swing between pricing escalation and diplomacy, and haven assets such as gold and the US dollar are likely to stay supported while uncertainty persists.

---

Earlier:

  • Reports: US reduces troops and diplomats across Middle East amid threat of military action on Iran

---

Washington and Israel are ready to go back to war with Iran after the midterms, if Trump does not call it off again, and Tehran is signalling that oil prices will be its weapon of choice in reply.

Summary:

  • The US and Israeli militaries have drawn up specific plans for renewed strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections, the New York Times (gated) reported, citing US officials and others briefed on the deliberations
  • Likely targets include Iran’s nuclear facilities, missile and drone arsenal and energy infrastructure, though some officials say refineries and oil infrastructure would be avoided to limit gasoline price rises
  • The US military buildup, including three aircraft carriers, is expected to be fully in place by early November
  • Trump has repeatedly vetoed a return to major combat, including earlier this month when both militaries were nearly ready to strike
  • Iranian figures have threatened to retaliate against Saudi oil refineries, data centres and undersea internet cables
  • Israel’s October 27 election could complicate the plans; the White House declined to comment on military planning

The US and Israeli militaries have developed specific plans for renewed strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections, the New York Times reported, citing US officials and other people briefed on the deliberations.

According to the report, planning is focused on a short but intensive operation, and the two militaries have stepped up exercises, including practice strike flights over Iraq. US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel this week to discuss new strikes, officials said. Likely targets include Iran’s nuclear facilities, its missile and drone arsenal and its energy infrastructure. However, some officials said targeting would avoid refineries and oil infrastructure because President Donald Trump is keen to prevent further rises in gasoline prices. Some US planners believe a three-day campaign could inflict enough economic damage to shift Iran’s negotiating position.

The US is assembling forces, including three aircraft carriers, thousands of Marines, fighter jets and special operations units, which are expected to be fully in place by early November. Officials said there is a small possibility of action this month, but Trump is likely to wait until after the election, having promised not to strike before the vote.

It is far from certain that Trump will approve new strikes. He has repeatedly vetoed plans for a return to major combat this year, including earlier this month, when the US and Israeli militaries were nearly ready to attack. The White House said it does not comment on military plans and that all options remain on the table to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons.

The newspaper noted reasons for scepticism. The first phase of intense strikes, between February and April, drove up energy prices and inflation globally and strained US supplies of missile interceptors, while Iran’s government has so far withstood economic pressure. Iranian negotiators have refused to make concessions on the nuclear programme, even as US negotiators use the threat of renewed war as leverage in talks that also cover control of the Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian figures have warned of wider retaliation. One Tehran-based analyst said Iran could target major Saudi oil refineries, including Aramco facilities, to push up energy prices, and officials have pointed to data centres and undersea internet cables as possible new targets. Israel’s October 27 election could also complicate the timing, as a Netanyahu defeat would leave him as a caretaker leader.

The report comes after the US State Department ordered non-emergency staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, as Iran-backed Houthi forces continue to attack sites there. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
